newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Two new deputy governors named at BOE. [CORRECTED 10:21 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Two new deputy governors named at BOE. [CORRECTED 10:21 GMT]

text.p: Britain's new Labour government has reinforced its pro-business credentials by appointing David Clementi, a top investment banker and architect of Conservative privatisations, as deputy governor of the Bank of England.

Prime Minister Tony Blair's office also said that the central bank's chief economist Mervyn King, an inflation hawk, would be appointed as second deputy governor in charge of monetary policy in the autumn.
Clementi will succeed Howard Davies who is leaving to head a revamped City watchdog, the Securities and Investment Board (SIB).
Davies was also an "outsider" at the central bank, having been head-hunted from the Confederation of British Industry, where he had been director general.
Clementi, 48, will join the nine-member Monetary Policy Committee, which sets interest rates, in time for its next monthly meeting on September 10 and 11 (corrects from August 6 and 7).
He spent 22 years at merchant bank Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, including three years as chief executive, which culminated in his appointment as vice chairman this year.

The appointment of someone who played a prominent role in the former Conservative government's 1980s privatisation programme underlines just how much has changed under New Labour. The party was once implacably opposed to privatisation and firmly wedded to the doctrine of national ownership of key industries and utilities.

As leader of the day-to-day team responsible for advising Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government on privatisation, Clementi spearheaded the sales of British Telecom, British Gas and the more controversial sell-off of the electricity industry.

Within the corporate finance department of Kleinwort, he also advised on the flotations of Laura Ashley, TV-am, and Abbey National as well as advising a wide range of companies on international equity issues.
Clementi, who was born in Bury, Northern England, trained as a chartered accountant with Arthur Andersen and has an MBA from Harvard Business School.
Former Bank of England officials say Clementi's job is the less glamorous of the two deputy governor positions.
King, 49, will be responsible "for analysis and advice in relation to the bank's responsibilities for delivering the government's inflation target," Blair's office said.
King has been with the central bank for seven years and was previously professor of economics at the London School of Economics.

But in taking over from Davies as head of internal management at the central bank -- effectively a chief executive's role -- Clementi will have more than enough to do overseeing the current reorganisation of the central bank.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown in May gave the bank operational responsibility for setting interest rates but also announced that much of its regulatory role would be transferred to the SIB, while the Treasury will take over debt management.
The last big internal reshuffle of the bank was presided over by Davies' predecessor Rupert Pennant-Rea, who quit after a sex scandal.

Clementi's move from the private to the public sector will mean a substantial pay cut, but his deputy governor's salary of 184,000 pounds ($300,000) per year is still just under 11 times British national average earnings.
There has been some surprise over Clementi's appointment as he is widely known in corporate finance circles but less so in the British financial community generally.
Clementi is married with one daughter and one son. His interests include sailing and athletics. He was a member of the British Junior International Athletics team in 1968.

The bank's biographical sketch of King said "he would like to spend more time reading European history, listening to music and playing tennis, which he did regularly before the inflation target was introduced." ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
